During Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya holds authority, ordering Sitaram to open a door and then actively tying him up himself after Sitaram humbly yields his weapon. During Udayaditya's imprisonment, the roles reverse completely: Sitaram takes charge, breaks into the dark cell, urgently commands Udayaditya to leave, physically grabs him, and almost carries him to safety while the prince is forced into a passive, dependent role.

Pratapaditya's initial, failed plan was to have two Pathan men assassinate Basanta Ray when he sheltered at an inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. His death is ultimately brought about by execution with a sword: after Pratapaditya's signed death warrant is delivered via Muktiyar Khan, Basanta Ray consents to his fate and is killed by a man named Abdul who enters with a drawn sword.
Mahishi’s room (disguised as a middle-aged woman) and the king’s chamber (in his role as a jester).
The secret preparation of poison by Mangala (Rukmini) at the Mahishi's request to make Yubaraj fall in love with another woman.

Ramchandra Ray took another wife as revenge for the insult, and when Rammohan later returned to fetch Vibha, the king was already married and offered her no forgiveness, shattering her hopes of happiness.

Rukmini takes the ring and gives it to Sitaram and Bhagavat, who use its engraved seal to stamp a forged petition falsely accusing Udayaditya of treason. Bhagavat then presents this sealed document to Pratapaditya as evidence, leading him to order Udayaditya's imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray's escape caused Pratapaditya to become hyper-vigilant and pay special attention to Udayaditya. This heightened scrutiny enabled the Maharaj to quickly discover Surma’s secret financial assistance to dismissed palace guards. Interpreting her covert actions as defiance, he responded by issuing the decree ordering her exile to her paternal home.

The song emotionally signifies profound loneliness, grief, and the loss of shared joy due to the absence of loved ones who are no longer there to accompany him. Basanta Ray sings it first spontaneously while gazing at a setting sun on his Raigarh veranda, reflecting mournfully on fading past joys and absent companions in a moment of quiet sorrow. He sings it second time after visiting the devastated royal palace in Jessore, directly responding to the harsh confirmation that his family has been scattered or imprisoned, marking a contrast between reflective melancholy and the heart-rending realization of irreversible loss.
Rukmini’s failure forces her to reveal Udayaditya’s survival to Pratapaditya, who then secretly orders Muktiyar Khan to execute Basanta Ray. This exact order is later carried out against Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya initially receives Ramchandra with cold indifference and minimal ceremony, offering only a brief, casual greeting before immediately returning to his ministerial business without showing any special honor or attention. In stark contrast, at his own court in Rajpur, Ramchandra actively encourages daily mockery of Pratapaditya, laughs along as officials belittle his lineage and standing, and openly treats him as entirely inferior.

She moves to the outskirts of Jessore under the name Mangala, befriends palace servants to spy on court affairs, and exploits her knowledge of tantra, mantras, and medicine. To cause tragedy, she prepares a poison over five days while chanting spells specifically so Udayaditya will not pity Surma when she is ordered out of the palace. The poisoned medicine ultimately kills Surma. Afterward, she directly visits Udayaditya in his bedchamber at night, manipulating his emotions by accusing him of ruining her to reclaim his affection and influence.

Udayaditya's early lament reflects his lifelong belief that he lacks the strength and intellect for rulership and would have been better off as a lowly subject. This deep-seated sense of inadequacy, compounded by grief over past events and his conviction that he has caused ruin for others, culminates when he is brought before his father Pratapaditya as a prisoner. Acknowledging himself as unworthy of the kingdom, Udayaditya formally renounces his claim by swearing an oath before Ma-Kali that he will never accept any portion of the throne, will not sit on it or touch the royal scepter, and designates Samaraditya as the rightful heir, fearing that breaking this vow would make him responsible for his grand-uncle's murder.

Nayanchand intercepted the letter by diverting it from Pratapaditya to the Mahishi out of fear of the Maharaj's reaction. The Mahishi showed it to Basanta Ray, who misinterpreted Ramchandra’s insult as temporary anger and advised announcing that the letter was actually a request for Vibha's return. Consequently, the Mahishi told the household and Vibha that Ramchandra had written asking for her to be sent to Chandradwip, leading Vibha to believe he had forgiven her and wanted her back.

Pratapaditya ordered the canal adjoining the palace blocked with large sal wood logs to stop Ramchandra Ray’s boat. The trap fails because when Rammohan and his followers pull the boat up and over the log barrier, the guards lack gunpowder and bullets for their flintlock, wasting crucial time shouting for supplies. Additionally, the messenger sent to fetch a pursuit boat is delayed by smoking tobacco and pressing a debt, allowing the escaping party to slip away before any chase can be organized.

Basanta Ray's vow to leave the sitar behind and his later claim that its strings are broken and unplayable reflect his despair by showing that he has lost all joy in music since Udayaditya is gone. Despite physically possessing the instrument, he can no longer tune or play it because the person he used to perform for is absent, mirroring his profound emotional emptiness and grief over Udayaditya's imprisonment.

Earlier, Udayaditya was courageous and proactive, willing to stop officials without hesitation or concern for personal consequences to protect oppressed subjects and actively involve himself in their affairs. After Surma's death, a paralyzing fear of Pratapaditya takes hold, causing his former courage to vanish; he now hesitates in every task, flees into his house when witnessing injustice instead of intervening, and loses the resolve to help those in financial hardship, effectively abandoning his previous willingness to defend his subjects out of sheer terror.
He frees Udayaditya from prison by grabbing him and carrying him out during a fire that erupts near the guards' huts, exploiting the chaos caused by the blaze.

On one occasion, he ties thick sheets together into a makeshift rope secured to the palace roof pillar, climbs down while carrying Ramchandra Ray on his back, and lowers him into a waiting boat using his hands and teeth. On the second occasion, he physically lifts the fainted Vibha out of the palace room and carries her to a waiting palanquin.

In Jessore, Vibha is elaborately adorned with eight thick gold bangles and a diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and styled hair, presented joyfully as a celebrated royal bride. In Chandradwip, after learning she has been rejected, she deliberately dresses as a common woman or beggar-woman, refuses a palanquin, keeps her veil covering her face, enters the palace like an unacknowledged maidservant, and appears so shamed and destitute that the king mistakes her for a beggar seeking alms.

In his bedchamber, the window serves as a focal point for longing and grief, representing the empty space where Surma used to sit and sustaining a fleeting hope that she might return. In the prison cell, it transforms into a symbol of hope and spiritual liberation; gazing through it at the sky and birds reminds him that his physical captivity is temporary, keeps despair and darkness at bay, and sustains his sense of inherent freedom despite his chains.

Initially, Sitaram repeatedly borrows money from Rukmini while engaging in constant flirtatious banter and affectionate nicknames, with her allowing his unpaid debts to accumulate through feigned affection and playful jokes about interest. The dynamic shifts when the Yubaraj is imprisoned; Sitaram angrily confronts Rukmini, vowing to free him and punish her, which reveals her concealed resentment. After Sitaram successfully orchestrates the Yubaraj's escape and stages a palace fire to fake his death, he visits Rukmini’s house opportunistically to steal her savings. Instead of being subdued, he finds her looking spectral and despondent. She reveals she knows everything about the escape, declares her vengeful intentions toward both him and the Yubaraj, and when Sitaram attempts to calm her with feigned affection, she furiously grabs a curved blade and chases him out as he narrowly escapes and flees Jessore, fully transforming their relationship from playful financial entanglement into a deadly confrontation.

Sitaram's strategy begins by intentionally igniting multiple rooms simultaneously to create widespread chaos, drawing all guards' attention away from the prison. His accomplices actively sabotage firefighting efforts by pouring water on non-burning areas, breaking pots, and causing confusion. While the guards are occupied with this distraction, his men set fire specifically to Udayaditya's already emptied cell. To transform the distraction into a cover-up, Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and the Yubaraj's sword into the burning room, then spreads panic by claiming screams were heard from inside. Guards rush to the cell, see the collapsed structure, and assume the prince perished. The fabricated evidence of burnt remains and false witness accounts successfully convinces the king that Udayaditya died in the fire, completely masking his escape.

Ramchandra Ray interpreted the actions with complete lack of gratitude, believing it was only natural that anyone would save him and assuming Udayaditya acted solely out of concern for his sister rather than loyalty to Ramchandra himself. As a result, he dismissed the rescue entirely and used his court sessions to mock and joke about Udayaditya for the "crime" of being Pratapaditya’s son.

Conspirators forge a petition falsely claiming that Prince Udayaditya was lodging a treason complaint against his father with the Emperor of Delhi to seize the kingdom. Stamped with the prince's seal, Bhagavat secretly delivers this document to Pratapaditya, pretending he intercepted it from a fleeing servant who was taking it to Delhi.

In the provided text, Vibha's hair marks Surma's presence through the intimate care and personal preference she provided, as Vibha once secretly went to Surma to have her hair styled according to her own liking rather than accepting the Mahishi's forced adornment. Following Surma's tragic absence, the daily need to braid it becomes a visible marker of loss; each time it is time to braid her hair, Vibha waits in silence for Surma to return, only to find her hair left unbraided when she does not come, physically manifesting Vibha's lingering hope, waiting, and profound sorrow.
